sentence: The leading expert doubted it could ever be timed.
claim: Johannes Müller, the leading physiologist of the 1840s, held that the nerve signal was so fast it could never be measured.
source_title: Hermann von Helmholtz and the speed of the nerve impulse (University of Georgia, Department of Psychology, manuscript, 2019)
note: Excerpt: Müller reasoned that nerve conduction was extremely fast and would probably never be measured. Review fix: 'doubted', not 'swore'.

sentence: It's a nerve signal, racing down one cell's thin fibre.
claim: A nerve signal (action potential) travels along an axon, the long, thin projection of a single nerve cell, typically about a micrometre across.
source_title: Axon (Wikipedia)
note: Excerpt: most individual axons are microscopic in diameter, typically about one micrometer across, and some extend a metre or more.

sentence: Some fibres reach from spine to toe: about a metre.
claim: Some human axons run from the lower spinal cord to the toes, about a metre long.
source_title: BioNumbers 104901: length of neuron from base of spine to big toe, the longest cell in the human body
note: Excerpt: length of neuron from base of spine to big toe, range ≤1 metre. Guinness gives about 1.3 m for these motor neurons. The sensory fibres from the toe, running up the spinal cord to the brainstem, are longer still (about 1.5 m in an adult; Guinness, guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/67725-longest-cell, search excerpt: about the body's height), so these are not the longest (BioNumbers' own title says 'longest cell'; its ≤1 m is for this route only). 'About a metre' sits in the spine-to-toe range. 26 Oct audit: the line said 'Your longest run from spine to toe' and the readout 'longest nerve cell, about 1 m'; 'longest' is wrong (the toe's sensory fibres are longer) and 'Your longest run' was heard as a jog, so the line says 'Some fibres reach from spine to toe' and the readout 'spine to toe: about 1 m'.

sentence: Johannes Müller thought it might be as fast as light.
claim: Müller thought the nerve signal's speed might be of the order of the speed of light; he cited estimates up to 60 times the speed of light.
source_title: Hermann von Helmholtz and the speed of the nerve impulse (University of Georgia, Department of Psychology, manuscript, 2019)
note: Excerpt (UGA manuscript): Müller cited possible speeds up to 60 times the speed of light and thought conduction extremely fast. Review fix: the 60× figure was a cited estimate, not his own guess, so the line says 'might be as fast as light'.

sentence: Johannes Müller thought it might be as fast as light.
claim: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s (shown on screen as Müller's guess).
source_title: Speed of light in vacuum (NIST Reference on Constants, Units and Uncertainty; CODATA 2022)
note: A defined constant: 299 792 458 m/s exact. The readout rounds it to 300,000,000 m/s and labels it 'Müller wondered: as fast as light?', with the question mark: c4 says he thought it might be of that order (the 60× figure he cited was an estimate, not his own guess).

sentence: In eighteen fifty, his former student Helmholtz timed it.
claim: In January 1850 Hermann Helmholtz, who had trained under Müller in Berlin, reported measuring the nerve's conduction speed with a frog nerve-muscle preparation.
source_title: Hermann von Helmholtz and the speed of the nerve impulse (University of Georgia, Department of Psychology, manuscript, 2019)
note: Excerpt: Helmholtz sent a short note on 15 January 1850 to du Bois-Reymond and to Müller; frog nerve-muscle preparation. Müller supervised Helmholtz's doctorate; in 1850 Helmholtz was a professor at Königsberg, hence 'former student' (review fix; BYU-Idaho history of psychology agrees). The frog's nerve-muscle preparation is shown (an illustration) rather than said.

sentence: About thirty metres a second: cheetah speed.
claim: Helmholtz's frog measurement came to roughly 27 m/s (about 90 ft/s); his reported values span about 25–43 m/s.
source_title: Hermann von Helmholtz and the speed of the nerve impulse (University of Georgia, Department of Psychology, manuscript, 2019)
note: Excerpt: 'roughly 90 feet per second' (= 27.4 m/s, computed); Schmidgen's account gives 25–43 m/s. 'About thirty' covers it. The drum is an illustration of his method (badged 'illustration · delay exaggerated' top right and 'slowed' top left): the far stimulus's later rise is drawn far wider than the real few thousandths of a second.

sentence: About thirty metres a second: cheetah speed.
claim: A cheetah's top speed is roughly 26–29 m/s: wild cheetahs measured up to about 25.9 m/s, captive ones up to about 29 m/s.
source_title: Cheetahs' speed is only half the story (National Geographic, 2013, on Wilson et al., Nature)
note: Excerpt (National Geographic on Wilson et al. 2013, Nature): wild cheetahs' fastest 25.9 m/s (58 mph, 93 km/h); captive cheetahs in straight runs up to 29 m/s. So about 30 m/s is cheetah speed (computed comparison).

sentence: It isn't current in a wire: the cell re-fires it, step by step.
claim: An action potential is not carried passively like current in a wire (which would fade over distance); it is regenerated by voltage-gated ion channels in each successive patch of membrane, which is why conduction is far slower than electricity in a wire.
source_title: Action potential conduction (Indiana University, Human Physiology open textbook)
note: Bible S13; excerpt: the action potential is regenerated as it travels; in myelinated axons it is regenerated at each node. Purves (NBK10921) agrees: passive current flow alone decays with distance, so the signal is regenerated along the way. 'Step by step' = patch by patch of membrane.

sentence: Many of your fibres wear fatty myelin, re-firing only at gaps, so the signal leaps.
claim: Many vertebrate axons are wrapped in myelin, an insulating sheath of membrane layers made by glial cells (oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells), interrupted by bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier.
source_title: Purves et al., Neuroscience 2nd ed., Increased Conduction Velocity as a Result of Myelination (NCBI Bookshelf NBK10921)
note: Excerpt: myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS); the gaps are the nodes of Ranvier. 'Fatty': myelin is a lipid-rich membrane (standard description). 'Many of your fibres': not all axons are myelinated. 26 Oct audit: 'Many of yours' had no noun a listener could point it back to (the sentence before ends on 'wire' and 'cell'), so it names the fibres; myelin wraps the fibre (axon), not the cell.

sentence: Many of your fibres wear fatty myelin, re-firing only at gaps, so the signal leaps.
claim: In myelinated axons action potentials are generated only at the nodes of Ranvier; current flows passively under the myelin to the next node, so the signal appears to jump (saltatory conduction).
source_title: Purves et al., Neuroscience 2nd ed., Increased Conduction Velocity as a Result of Myelination (NCBI Bookshelf NBK10921)
note: Excerpt: action potentials are generated only at the nodes; current passes passively to the next node, where the cycle repeats. 'Leaps' is the textbook picture; ions do not physically jump. 26 Oct audit: 'Many of yours' became 'Many of your fibres' (wording only).

sentence: Where myelin is damaged, as in multiple sclerosis, signals can slow or stall.
claim: In multiple sclerosis, damage to myelin disrupts or slows nerve signals; signals can be slowed, garbled or blocked.
source_title: Multiple sclerosis (Harvard Health Publishing)
note: Excerpt (Harvard Health): damage to myelin disrupts or slows nerve signals. MSD Manuals: signals slowed, garbled or blocked. NINDS: MS attacks myelinated axons in the CNS. 'Can' and 'stall' (= blocked) keep it to the sources. No advice. MS affects the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves (NINDS), so the shot is labelled a brain-and-spinal-cord fibre (review fix).

sentence: The thinnest bare fibres crawl at about a metre a second.
claim: Unmyelinated C fibres conduct at about 0.5–2 m/s (typically about 1 m/s); unmyelinated axons in general 0.5–10 m/s.
source_title: Pain (Introduction to Neuroscience, Michigan State University Libraries open textbook)
note: Excerpt: C fibres slow, about 0.5–2 m/s (~1 m/s typical). Review fix: 'the thinnest bare fibres' (bare fibres in general run 0.5–10 m/s, NBK10921).

sentence: Thick wrapped ones, up to a hundred and fifty.
claim: Myelinated axons conduct at up to about 150 m/s; the fastest are the thickest.
source_title: Purves et al., Neuroscience 2nd ed., Increased Conduction Velocity as a Result of Myelination (NCBI Bookshelf NBK10921)
note: Excerpt (NBK10921): myelinated axons up to 150 m/s; bare ones 0.5–10 m/s. 'Up to' = the top of the range, reached by the thickest wrapped fibres (A-alpha, about 13–20 µm). 26 Oct audit: the line said 'Wrapped ones', which set the thinnest bare fibres against the fastest wrapped ones and left the whole gap to myelin. Part of it is thickness: speed grows with the square root of a bare fibre's diameter and roughly in proportion to a wrapped one's (McGill, The Brain from Top to Bottom, thebrain.mcgill.ca/flash/a/a_01/a_01_cl/a_01_cl_fon/a_01_cl_fon.html, search excerpt: speed proportional to diameter if myelinated, only to its square root if not), so at equal thickness myelin gives roughly 20–30 times (a 15–20 µm bare fibre would run about 4 m/s, a wrapped one about 90–120 m/s; the audit's arithmetic), not 150; the rest is thickness. The line now says 'Thick wrapped ones' and the race draws the wrapped fibre thicker.

sentence: Faster than a Formula One car.
claim: 150 m/s is 540 km/h; the fastest speed recorded in a Formula One Grand Prix is 372.6 km/h.
source_title: Fastest speed outright in a Formula One Grand Prix (Guinness World Records)
note: Excerpt: 372.6 km/h (231.5 mph), Juan Pablo Montoya, McLaren-Mercedes, Monza, 4 September 2005. Computed: 150 m/s × 3.6 = 540 km/h > 372.6 km/h. (Bottas's 378 km/h in 2016 was team data, not the official trap.)

sentence: So a stubbed toe can hurt twice.
claim: A painful stimulus far from the brain, such as a stubbed toe, is often felt as two pains: a sharp first pain, then a dull, aching second pain.
source_title: Pain (Introduction to Neuroscience, Michigan State University Libraries open textbook)
note: Excerpt: first pain (thinly myelinated A-delta, about 5–25 m/s) precedes second pain (unmyelinated C, about 0.5–2 m/s), easiest to tell apart far from the brain. Computed: over about 1.5 m, about 0.1 s (at 15 m/s) against about 1.5 s (at 1 m/s). Review fix: 'faster' fibres (A-delta are thinly myelinated, not the 150 m/s fibres) and 'can hurt twice'. 26 Oct audit: the next sentence (c19) now says 'faster fibres', not 'faster wires'.

sentence: The jolt rides faster fibres; the ache, bare ones.
claim: Painful stimuli are carried by thinly myelinated A-delta fibres (about 5–25 m/s), giving a sharp, well-localised first pain, and by unmyelinated C fibres (about 0.5–2 m/s), giving a dull, aching second pain that follows; the delay is easiest to notice far from the brain.
source_title: Pain (Introduction to Neuroscience, Michigan State University Libraries open textbook)
note: Excerpt: first pain (thinly myelinated A-delta, about 5–25 m/s) precedes second pain (unmyelinated C, about 0.5–2 m/s), easiest to tell apart far from the brain. Computed: over about 1.5 m, about 0.1 s (at 15 m/s) against about 1.5 s (at 1 m/s). Review fix: 'faster' fibres (A-delta are thinly myelinated, not the 150 m/s fibres) and 'can hurt twice'. The on-screen timer stops at 2.2 s (the slow signal lands on the spoken 'ache'): computed, 2.2 s over about 1.6 m toe to brain is about 0.73 m/s, inside the C-fibre range of 0.5–2 m/s (0.8–3.2 s over 1.6 m). 26 Oct audit: 'faster wires' became 'faster fibres' (the why has just said the signal isn't current in a wire).

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, a heart at rest beat about eighty times.
claim: A normal resting heart rate for adults is 60–100 beats a minute; the tally uses 75 a minute (the channel's tempo).
source_title: What's a normal resting heart rate? (Mayo Clinic)
note: Excerpt: 'A normal resting heart rate for adults ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute.' The tally is 75/60 × t beats from frame 0; the line lands near 64 s, about 80 (computed). At 60–100 a minute the same span gives 64–107, so 'a resting heart … about eighty' is an example, not the viewer's own.

sentence: Each began with a spark.
claim: Each heartbeat is initiated by an electrical impulse from the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker.
source_title: Physiology, Sinoatrial Node (StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK459238)
note: Excerpt (StatPearls): the SA node is the primary pacemaker, generating the impulses that start each heartbeat. Bible S23. Sets up episode 7. 'Spark' = the electrical impulse.

sentence: A gap most signals can't jump.
claim: At most synapses (chemical synapses) the electrical signal does not cross the narrow synaptic cleft: it is converted into a chemical signal, neurotransmitter released into the gap.
source_title: Physiology, Synapse (StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK526047)
note: Excerpt (StatPearls Synapse): chemical synapses pass the signal as neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft; electrical synapses also exist, hence 'most' (review fix). Episode 4 tells it.
